etymology: Greek Mura, a seaport of Lycia on the southern coast of Asia Minor. A station on the grain route between Egypt and Italy.
biblical_def: Myra was a port city of Lycia on the southern coast of Asia Minor, and a way-station on Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner. Sailing from Caesarea under the centurion Julius, Paul's company coasted along Asia and came to Myra, "and there the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing into Italy; and he put us therein" (Acts 27:5-6). The great Alexandrian grain ships that fed Rome commonly put in at the Lycian harbors, and it was such a vessel — later wrecked off Malta — that carried Paul toward the capital. Myra is thus a hinge in the providential journey by which the apostle reached Rome to testify of Christ before Caesar, fulfilling the Lord's word: "so must thou bear witness also at Rome" (Acts 23:11). Though only a sentence of Scripture mentions it, Myra marks the quiet outworking of God's purpose: a prisoner in chains, transferred from ship to ship at an obscure harbor, was being carried by unseen sovereignty to the heart of the empire, that the gospel might be preached in Caesar's own household. Every change of vessel, every wind and harbor, served the design of the God who had promised Paul his testimony in Rome.
webster_summary: A Lycian seaport (Acts 27:5-6) where the centurion transferred Paul to an Alexandrian grain ship bound for Italy; a quiet hinge in the providential voyage carrying the apostle to testify at Rome.

corruption_summary: Myra needs little defense from redefinition; the principle to recover is the doctrine of providence — that God governs the obscure details of harbors, ships, and winds to accomplish His revealed purposes.
corruption_paragraphs: Providence-flattened misreading. A merely secular history sees in Myra only a routine transfer of cargo and prisoners. Scripture sets the same event within the announced purpose of God: Paul must bear witness at Rome, and every harbor served that end. The dictionary holds that providence is not a pious afterthought but the actual government of God over all second causes — winds, centurions, grain ships — bending them, without violence to their nature, toward His appointed ends.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery it calls for is confidence in divine sovereignty over ordinary means. The believer carried by circumstances he did not choose may, like Paul at Myra, trust that the God who promised his arrival governs every transfer along the way. Nothing in the journey is wasted, and nothing is outside the Father's hand.

etymology: A translation of the Greek Kaloi Limenes, "Fair Havens," a roadstead on the south coast of Crete near the city of Lasea.
biblical_def: Fair Havens was an anchorage on the southern coast of Crete where Paul's grain ship sheltered as the sailing season grew dangerous. "And, hardly passing it, came unto a place which is called The fair havens; nigh whereunto was the city of Lasea" (Acts 27:8). Here Paul, though a prisoner, gave counsel born of experience and of God: "Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage, not only of the lading and ship, but also of our lives" (Acts 27:10). But the centurion believed the master and owner of the ship rather than the apostle, and because the haven was "not commodious to winter in," the majority resolved to sail on toward Phenice. That decision led straight into the tempest Euroclydon and the wreck off Malta. Fair Havens is therefore a place of solemn instruction: the safe harbor refused, the inspired warning overruled by the consensus of experts and the pressure of convenience. Yet even the disregard of Paul's counsel did not defeat God's purpose; the Lord would later send His angel to promise that not one life would be lost. Fair Havens stands as a warning against despising godly counsel for the sake of comfort, and a testimony that God preserves His servants even through the storms their companions steer into.
webster_summary: A Cretan anchorage near Lasea (Acts 27:8) where Paul warned the voyage would bring loss of ship and life; his counsel was overruled for a more comfortable harbor, and the ship sailed on into the tempest and wreck.

corruption_summary: Fair Havens needs little defense from redefinition; its lesson is the danger of preferring expert consensus and comfort to godly counsel, and the faithfulness of God who preserves His own even through the storms of others' folly.
corruption_paragraphs: Counsel-despised misreading. The world reads Acts 27 as a tale of bad weather; Scripture frames it as a parable of disregarded warning. The centurion trusted the professionals and the convenient harbor over the man of God, and sailed into ruin. The dictionary holds the abiding lesson: the consensus of the skilled and the pull of comfort are no substitute for the counsel of the godly, and to overrule the latter for the former is a perennial temptation of leadership.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, wisdom may speak from the prisoner and be ignored by the powerful; the value of counsel is not measured by the rank of the counselor. Second, God's preserving mercy is not cancelled by human folly — He sent His angel to Paul in the very storm the others had chosen, and saved all aboard for the sake of His servant. Refused havens do not thwart His purposes.

etymology: Greek Lasaia, a city on the southern coast of Crete, near the anchorage of Fair Havens.
biblical_def: Lasea was a city on the south coast of Crete, named in Scripture only as the landmark nearest the anchorage of Fair Havens: "a place which is called The fair havens; nigh whereunto was the city of Lasea" (Acts 27:8). It belongs to the closely observed record of Paul's voyage to Rome, where Luke, the careful eyewitness physician, sets down the coastline, harbors, winds, and soundings with the exactness of a man who was there. Lasea's single mention is a quiet testimony to the historical precision of the Acts narrative. The voyage of Acts 27 is among the most detailed and verifiable accounts of ancient seafaring that survives, and its incidental notices — a small city beside a roadstead, the changing winds, the depth of the water near Malta — bear the marks of sober history, not legend. Lasea reminds the reader that the saving acts of God were done in real places, on real coasts, witnessed and recorded by men who handled what they had seen. The same Spirit who inspired the doctrine of the epistles guided the pen that noted a Cretan town beside a harbor, that the whole account might stand as truth.
webster_summary: A city on the south coast of Crete named only as the landmark nearest Fair Havens (Acts 27:8); a quiet witness to the eyewitness precision of Luke's record of Paul's voyage.

corruption_summary: Lasea needs no defense from redefinition; its single mention rebukes the notion that the Bible's narratives are myth, testifying instead to the eyewitness historicity of the record.
corruption_paragraphs: Myth-theory misreading. Liberal criticism has often treated the Gospels and Acts as legendary constructions far removed from real events. The incidental geography of Acts 27 — a small Cretan city beside a harbor, named because it was simply there — tells against that theory. Such offhand precision is the signature of testimony, not invention. The dictionary holds with the church that Luke wrote "in order" what eyewitnesses delivered (Luke 1:1-4), and that the historicity of Scripture is part of its authority.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the trustworthiness of the biblical record in its smallest details. A faith founded on real events in real places can be confessed without embarrassment; the God of the Bible acted in history and had it written down by men who saw. Lasea, mentioned once and never again, is a small stone in the firm foundation of that confidence.

etymology: Greek Klauda (also Cauda), a small island off the southwest coast of Crete, under whose lee Paul's ship ran during the tempest.
biblical_def: Clauda was a small island southwest of Crete that gave Paul's storm-driven ship a brief shelter during the tempest called Euroclydon. When the violent wind seized the vessel and they could not bear up into it, "we let her drive. And running under a certain island which is called Clauda, we had much work to come by the boat" (Acts 27:15-16). Under the island's lee the sailors hauled in the ship's boat with difficulty, undergirded the hull with cables to hold it together, and struck sail, fearing the quicksands of the Syrtis. Clauda marks the moment the crew passed from confidence to desperation: the next day they lightened the ship, and the third day cast out its tackling with their own hands, until "all hope that we should be saved was then taken away" (Acts 27:20). It was into that hopelessness that God spoke, sending His angel to stand by Paul and promise, "Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee" (Acts 27:24). Clauda is thus the threshold of extremity, the brief shelter before the worst, where human skill was exhausted so that divine deliverance might be seen for what it was — the gift of God, granted for the sake of His servant.
webster_summary: A small island off southwest Crete (Acts 27:16) under whose lee Paul's ship found brief shelter in the tempest; the threshold of the crew's despair, just before God's angel promised that all aboard would be saved for Paul's sake.

corruption_summary: Clauda needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that God often lets human strength be exhausted to the point of despair so that His deliverance may be received as sheer grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-sufficiency misreading. A man-centered reading makes the survival of Acts 27 a triumph of seamanship and nerve. Scripture tells it the other way: all hope was taken away, and then God spoke and saved them. The dictionary holds that the Lord frequently brings His people past the end of their own resources, not to abandon them but to teach them that salvation is of the Lord. Clauda's brief shelter only delayed the moment when skill ran out and grace took over.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pattern of divine deliverance: extremity first, then mercy, that the glory may be God's. The promise given at the storm's worst — not one life lost — was grounded not in the crew's competence but in God's purpose for Paul. Those who sailed with the servant of God were spared for his sake, a quiet picture of the many preserved through the one.

etymology: Greek Melite, the island now called Malta, in the central Mediterranean south of Sicily, where Paul was shipwrecked and wintered.
biblical_def: Melita, the island now called Malta, was the place of Paul's shipwreck on the voyage to Rome, where all two hundred seventy-six souls aboard came safe to land, exactly as God had promised (Acts 27:44; 28:1). The "barbarous people" of the island "shewed us no little kindness: for they kindled a fire, and received us every one, because of the present rain, and because of the cold" (Acts 28:2). As Paul laid a bundle of sticks on the fire, a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened on his hand; the natives, seeing the venomous beast hang from him, judged him a murderer whom justice would not let live. But Paul "shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm" (Acts 28:5), and when he did not swell or fall dead, they changed their minds and said he was a god. On the island Paul healed the father of Publius, the chief man, who lay sick of a fever and bloody flux, and then all the diseased of the island came and were healed (Acts 28:8-9). After three months they departed, the islanders honoring them and supplying their need. Melita displays the keeping power of God promised in the storm, the fulfillment of the Lord's word that the gospel's bearer was immune to the serpent's sting (Mark 16:18), and the mercy of Christ flowing even to a barbarous island through His chained apostle.
webster_summary: The island (modern Malta) of Paul's shipwreck (Acts 28:1), where all 276 aboard came safe to land as God promised; the viper that did him no harm, the healing of Publius's father, and three months of mercy to the islanders display God's keeping power and the gospel's advance.

corruption_summary: Melita is corrupted when the miracle of the viper and the healings are explained away as luck or legend, denying the supernatural preservation and power God displayed through His apostle.
corruption_paragraphs: Miracle-denied misreading. Naturalism reduces the viper episode to a non-venomous snake or a lucky escape, and the healings to coincidence or folklore. Luke, a physician, records a venomous beast fastened on Paul's hand and a man healed of fever and dysentery by prayer and the laying on of hands. The dictionary holds these as real miracles, signs confirming the apostolic word (Heb 2:3-4) and fulfilling the Lord's promise that His messengers would be kept from deadly harm (Mark 16:18). To strip them of the supernatural is to rewrite the text.

Beyond the miracle, this entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the breadth of God's mercy: the gospel's keeping and healing power reached even a "barbarous" island through a prisoner in chains. The God who preserved every soul in the storm poured kindness on the shipwrecked and health on the sick, that Christ might be made known where He had not been named. No people is too remote, and no servant too bound, for the purposes of God.

etymology: Greek Surakousai, a leading city on the eastern coast of Sicily, a port of call on the last leg of Paul's voyage to Rome.
biblical_def: Syracuse was a principal city on the eastern coast of Sicily, where Paul's ship tarried three days on the final stretch of the voyage to Rome. After wintering at Malta, the company embarked in another Alexandrian ship, the Castor and Pollux, "and landing at Syracuse, we tarried there three days" (Acts 28:12). The brief notice belongs to the steady march of providence carrying Paul to the capital, port by port: Syracuse, then Rhegium, then Puteoli, and so toward Rome. Syracuse was a famous and ancient city, once a great power of the Greek world; yet in the sacred record it is simply a three-day harbor on the apostle's road. The juxtaposition is instructive. The cities men reckon great pass through the pages of Scripture as way-stations, while the purpose of God — the gospel borne to Rome by a chained witness — is the true greatness the narrative pursues. Wherever the ship touched, it carried the treasure of the testimony of Christ. Syracuse marks one more step of the journey the Lord had appointed, the unhurried, certain progress of His servant toward the throne of Caesar and the preaching of the kingdom in the heart of the empire.
webster_summary: A leading city of eastern Sicily where Paul's ship tarried three days (Acts 28:12) on the last leg of the voyage to Rome; a way-station in the steady providence carrying the apostle to the capital.

corruption_paragraphs: Greatness-misjudged reading. The world measures greatness by the power and fame of cities like Syracuse. Scripture quietly reorders the scale: the famous city is a three-day harbor, while the chained prisoner carries the one thing of eternal weight. The dictionary holds that the kingdom of God advances through what the world overlooks, and that the true significance of a place in the divine record is its service to the gospel's progress, not its standing among men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the routes and timing of His mission. Three days at Syracuse, one at Rhegium, seven at Puteoli — every pause was measured, every harbor appointed, that the testimony of Christ might reach Rome in God's own time. The believer may trust the same governance over the stages and delays of his own appointed course.

etymology: Greek Rhegion, a port city at the toe of Italy, on the strait opposite Sicily, a station on Paul's final approach to Rome.
biblical_def: Rhegium was a harbor city at the southwestern tip of Italy, on the strait separating the mainland from Sicily, where Paul's ship touched on its way up the coast to Puteoli. "And from thence we fetched a compass, and came to Rhegium: and after one day the south wind blew, and we came the next day to Puteoli" (Acts 28:13). The ship had waited at Rhegium for a favorable wind, and when the south wind came it carried them swiftly northward. The detail is one more mark of Luke's exact seamanship and of the providence governing the voyage: the very winds served the appointed end. After the long fight against contrary gales that had wrecked them off Malta, a fair south wind now sped the apostle toward Rome. Rhegium is the place where the journey, so long delayed and storm-tossed, turned at last toward its goal with the wind at their back. It pictures the truth that the same God who appoints the storms appoints the favoring breeze, and that the believer's course, however contrary the winds have been, will be brought home in God's good time. The Lord who had promised Paul his witness at Rome now sped him there on a southern wind.
webster_summary: A port at the toe of Italy on the Sicilian strait (Acts 28:13) where Paul's ship waited a day for the south wind that then sped them to Puteoli; the favoring breeze that turned the long voyage toward its goal.

corruption_paragraphs: Chance-attributed misreading. The secular eye sees only meteorology in the south wind at Rhegium. Scripture sees the hand of God, who "maketh the storm a calm" and "bringeth them unto their desired haven" (Psa 107:29-30). The dictionary holds that winds and weather are not autonomous forces but servants of providence; the gale that wrecked the ship and the breeze that sped it were alike under the government of the God who had appointed Paul's arrival at Rome.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is patience under contrary winds and confidence in the favoring ones. After long delay and disaster, the voyage turned toward its goal at Rhegium with the wind astern. The believer whose course has been long buffeted may take heart: the God who rules the storms also sends the south wind, and will bring His own to the haven He has appointed.

etymology: Greek Potioloi, a major port on the Bay of Naples in Italy, the chief landing for the Alexandrian grain fleet and the place where Paul first found brethren in Italy.
biblical_def: Puteoli was the principal port on the Bay of Naples and the usual landing for the great grain ships from Egypt, where Paul came ashore in Italy and found fellow believers. "And the next day we came to Puteoli: where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome" (Acts 28:13-14). The discovery is striking: before the apostle reached the capital, the gospel had already run ahead of him to this Italian harbor, and a company of brethren welcomed the prisoner and his companions. That they could persuade the centurion to let Paul stay seven days shows the favor God gave His servant even in chains. Puteoli testifies that the church of Christ was already scattered through the empire by ordinary believers — merchants, sailors, travelers — long before any apostle arrived, and that the fellowship of the saints spans every distance. A bound man, shipwrecked and weary, stepped onto Italian soil and was met as a brother by people he had never seen, bound to him by one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Puteoli is a picture of the communion of saints: the family of God receiving its own, refreshing the traveler, and speeding him on his way.

Puteoli tells otherwise: brethren were already gathered in an Italian port before Paul or any apostle came, the fruit of ordinary believers carrying Christ along the trade routes. The dictionary holds that the Great Commission is fulfilled not only through appointed leaders but through the scattered saints who bear witness wherever providence sends them; the church at Puteoli was such fruit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the communion of saints, that real and tender bond by which believers receive one another as family across every barrier of distance and acquaintance. A chained stranger was welcomed as a brother and kept seven days. etymology: Latin Appii Forum, "the Market of Appius," a town on the Appian Way about forty miles south of Rome, where Roman brethren came to meet Paul.
biblical_def: Appii Forum was a town on the Appian Way, some forty miles south of Rome, where believers from the capital came out to meet Paul as he approached on foot. "And from thence, when the brethren heard of us, they came to meet us as far as Appii forum, and The three taverns: whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage" (Acts 28:15). The scene is deeply moving. The apostle who had longed for years to see the Roman Christians (Rom 1:10-11; 15:23-24) was coming at last — not as he had hoped, a free preacher, but as a prisoner in chains. Yet the brethren did not wait at the city; they walked a day's journey down the great road to welcome him, and the sight of them lifted his heart: "he thanked God, and took courage." Appii Forum testifies to the strengthening power of Christian fellowship. The mere sight of brethren, who had come so far to honor a man they knew only by his letter to them, turned the prisoner's weariness to thanksgiving and his discouragement to courage. It shows that the people of God minister to one another not only by word and deed but by presence; that to come and stand beside a suffering saint is itself a gift of grace; and that even an apostle was refreshed by the love of the brethren.

corruption_paragraphs: Self-sufficiency misreading. A hyper-spiritual individualism imagines the mature believer needing no one. Yet the apostle Paul, on seeing the brethren, "thanked God, and took courage." The dictionary holds that God ordains the fellowship of the saints as a real means of strength; even the strongest servant is refreshed by the presence and love of God's people, and to despise that ministry is to despise a gift the Lord Himself has given.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ministry of mere presence. The Roman brethren preached no sermon and worked no wonder; they simply walked forty miles to stand beside a prisoner, and it was enough to turn his heart to thanksgiving. To go to the suffering, to be present with the weary, to honor the chained saint by coming — this is a grace the church must not neglect, for by it Paul himself took courage.

etymology: A translation of the Latin Tres Tabernae, "Three Taverns," a halting-place on the Appian Way about thirty miles south of Rome.
biblical_def: Three Taverns was a stopping-place on the Appian Way, about thirty miles south of Rome and nearer the city than Appii Forum, where a second company of Roman believers came to meet Paul on his journey to the capital. "They came to meet us as far as Appii forum, and The three taverns: whom when Paul saw, he thanked God, and took courage" (Acts 28:15). Two groups, it seems, had set out from Rome to welcome the apostle: one reaching the farther town, another waiting at the nearer halt. Both bore the same love, and the doubled welcome doubled the encouragement. Three Taverns shares with Appii Forum the witness to the refreshing power of Christian fellowship, but it adds its own note: the eagerness of the brethren, who could not all wait at the city but pressed out along the road to be the first to greet the man whose epistle to the Romans had so fed their souls. Here the great letter and its writer met. The church that had received the most weighty doctrinal epistle in the New Testament now received its author in person — a prisoner, footsore, in chains — and honored him with the only gift they could give: themselves, come out to meet him. Three Taverns marks the meeting of truth and love, of the apostle and the people his words had shaped.
webster_summary: A halt on the Appian Way thirty miles south of Rome (Acts 28:15) where a second company of Roman believers met Paul; with Appii Forum, the doubled welcome that turned the chained apostle's heart to thanksgiving and courage.

corruption_summary: Three Taverns needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the eagerness of Christian love, which presses out to meet the suffering saint, and the union of sound doctrine with warm affection.
corruption_paragraphs: Doctrine-versus-love misreading. Some imagine that a church devoted to weighty doctrine must be cold, and a warm church must be shallow. Three Taverns refutes the caricature: the very believers who had received the epistle to the Romans, the deepest doctrinal letter in the New Testament, were the ones who hurried down the road in love to meet its author. The dictionary holds that truth and love are not rivals but companions; the soundest doctrine, rightly received, produces the warmest affection.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the eagerness of love. The brethren did not wait passively but pressed out, some to the nearer halt and some to the farther, to be first to greet the prisoner. Such forward, seeking love — that will not wait to be sought but goes out to find and honor the servant of God — is the mark of a church shaped by the gospel it has believed.
